newsitem.title: USA: Florida pleased with U.S./Mexico tomato trade deal.
newsitem.headline: Florida pleased with U.S./Mexico tomato trade deal.

text.p: Florida Agriculture Commissioner Bob Crawford said Friday he was pleased that the U.S. government had reached an agreement to end the so-called "tomato war" with Mexico, and said he expected the pact would rejuvenate Florida's market.
"This ends a 20- to 30-year battle we've had on this front," Crawford told a news conference. "Our $800 million tomato industry will be allowed to get back on its feet."

Crawford said that in the past three years, the market for Florida tomatoes had dropped to about $400 million from $800 million, a drop he blamed almost completely on Mexican growers selling their tomatoes in the U.S. market for less than cost.

A group of growers filed a trade complaint charging Mexico with tomato dumping earlier this year. Crawford said the suit would be withdrawn because of the agreement reached by U.S. trade representatives and the Mexican government.
"We think we are making a very good case," Crawford said of the trade suit. "We believe that is why Mexico decided to come to the table."

Crawford said that without the agreement he believed that Florida's tomato industry would have ceased to exist. "It was getting to the point that within a year or two, you'd only have Mexican tomatoes here (the United States)," he said.

Under the proposed settlement, which was signed Thursday by U.S. officials and Mexican growers, Mexican tomato growers would agree to not sell their produce in the United States at less than a certain price, called the reference price.
The reference price is based on the lowest average Mexican import prices during a certain period, and can be adjusted after one year if market conditions change significantly.

Under the agreement, the U.S. government will implement a monitoring system of Mexican imports. The administration can terminate the agreement at any time if it finds that the terms have been violated.
